title: The tulip that broke the market

panels.text: Holland, 1636. Taverns fill with traders signing contracts for tulip bulbs not yet out of the ground. The most coveted flowers are streaked with flame-like colour.
The most famous, Semper Augustus, was said to sell for up to 10,000 guilders. A skilled craftsman earned roughly a tenth of that in a year.
The twist: those gorgeous streaks were a disease. A virus "broke" the petal colour, and it also weakened the bulb, so the prettiest tulips were the hardest to grow.
In February 1637 buyers stopped showing up and prices collapsed. Yet historian Anne Goldgar found that few people were actually ruined. The legend of a nation gone mad may be bigger than the bubble.

image.alt: Watercolour of a white tulip with red flame-like streaks, from the Tulip Book of the Six collection

probes.question: What really caused the famous flame-like streaks on the most prized tulips?
True or false: historian Anne Goldgar found that tulip mania ruined large numbers of ordinary Dutch people.
